headword: {良薬|りょうやく}{口|くち}に{苦|にが}し
reading: りょうやくくちににがし

definitions.gloss: good medicine tastes bitter; honest advice is hard to hear
definitions.explanation: Beneficial medicine is often unpleasant to take, just as truthful advice or constructive criticism can be difficult to accept. What helps us the most may not be comfortable.

examples.japanese: {良薬|りょうやく}{口|くち}に{苦|にが}しというから、{彼|かれ}の{厳|きび}しい{指摘|してき}も{素直|すなお}に{聞|き}こう。
examples.english: As they say, good medicine tastes bitter, so I'll accept his harsh criticism openly.

examples.japanese: {先生|せんせい}の{言葉|ことば}は{厳|きび}しいが、{良薬|りょうやく}{口|くち}に{苦|にが}しだ。
examples.english: The teacher's words are harsh, but good medicine tastes bitter.

examples.japanese: {良薬|りょうやく}{口|くち}に{苦|にが}しで、{本当|ほんとう}のことを{言|い}ってくれる{友人|ゆうじん}は{貴重|きちょう}だ。
examples.english: As the saying goes, good medicine is bitter—a friend who tells you the truth is precious.

notes:
ORIGIN: This proverb comes from Chinese (良药苦口), found in classical Chinese texts. It has been used in Japanese for centuries and is well-known.

FULL FORM: The complete version is {良薬|りょうやく}は{口|くち}に{苦|にが}けれども{病|やまい}に{利|き}あり、{忠言|ちゅうげん}は{耳|みみ}に{逆|さから}えども{行|おこな}いに{利|り}あり (Good medicine is bitter to the mouth but helps cure illness; honest advice is unpleasant to the ear but benefits one's conduct).

USAGE: Used when accepting or advising someone to accept constructive criticism, uncomfortable truths, or difficult but beneficial measures. Often quoted when someone receives harsh but fair feedback.

ENGLISH EQUIVALENTS:
・A bitter pill to swallow
・The truth hurts
・Tough love
